clinicalPearls: The finger catches, clicks, or locks in flexion and may need to be actively or passively straightened, often with pain at the base of the digit
The problem lies at the A1 pulley over the metacarpophalangeal joint, where the flexor tendon cannot glide smoothly through a narrowed sheath
A tender nodule may be palpable over the A1 pulley and can be felt to move with the tendon
Symptoms are frequently worse in the morning, with the digit locked, and it is most common in the thumb, ring, and middle fingers
It is associated with diabetes and inflammatory arthritis, and these patients tend to respond less well to conservative treatment
Severity is graded from painful catching without locking through to a fixed, non-reducible digit
Initial management includes activity modification and splinting, with corticosteroid injection into the sheath being effective in many cases
Injection tends to be less successful in people with diabetes and in longstanding or multiple-digit disease
Surgical or percutaneous release of the A1 pulley is used for cases that fail injection or present with fixed locking
reference.pathophysiology: Trigger finger is a stenosing tenosynovitis at the first annular (A1) pulley. Thickening and fibrocartilaginous change of the pulley and of the flexor tendon or its sheath create a mismatch in size, so the tendon catches as it passes through. A nodule on the tendon may become trapped proximal to the pulley, producing the characteristic triggering, locking, and pain, with a mechanical block rather than a simple inflammatory process.
additionalDifferentials: Focal dystonia or extensor tendon subluxation
Locked metacarpophalangeal joint from other causes
additionalInvestigations: A clinical diagnosis based on the history and demonstrable triggering
Ultrasound to confirm tendon or pulley thickening and guide injection in uncertain cases
Screening for diabetes given the association and its effect on outcome
Plain radiographs only if joint pathology is suspected
Assessment for inflammatory arthritis when multiple digits are affected
redFlags: Signs of flexor sheath infection such as fusiform swelling, severe pain on passive extension, and erythema
A fixed, non-reducible locked digit requiring timely surgical referral
Rapidly progressive or multi-digit involvement suggesting inflammatory arthritis
reference.prognosis: Many cases resolve with splinting or a single corticosteroid injection, though recurrence can occur; response is poorer in diabetic patients and longstanding disease, and surgical release is highly effective when needed.
pitfalls: Mistaking a locked digit for a joint problem rather than tendon triggering
Missing flexor sheath infection presenting with a swollen painful digit
Repeated injections in diabetic patients with limited benefit and glycaemic disturbance
Injuring the neurovascular bundle or digital nerve during release
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Begin conservative treatment with activity modification and a splint holding the metacarpophalangeal joint in extension, using NSAIDs for pain
Give a corticosteroid injection into the flexor tendon sheath at the A1 pulley as the mainstay of treatment, which is often curative
Refer for surgical A1 pulley release, open or percutaneous, for refractory triggering or a fixed, locked digit
Screen for and optimise diabetes and inflammatory arthritis, which are associated and predict a poorer response to conservative care
Provide hand therapy with tendon-gliding exercises to restore smooth excursion
Monitor for recurrence and escalate to surgical release when repeated injections fail
